text: When he learned that the boy had worked in the gasworks, Gabriel felt humiliated, for while he had been full of memories of their life together, she had been comparing him in her mind with another. <break time="0.8s" /> He saw himself as a ludicrous figure, a nervous, well meaning sentimentalist who made speeches to common people and idealized his own foolish desires, the pitiable fellow he had glimpsed in the mirror. <break time="0.8s" /> He tried to keep up a tone of cold questioning, but his voice was humble as he asked whether she had loved this Michael Furey, and she answered that she had been great with him then. <break time="0.8s" /> Feeling now how vain it would be to lead her where he had intended, Gabriel caressed one of her hands and asked sadly what the boy had died of at so young an age. <break time="0.8s" /> I think he died for me, she answered, and at those words a vague terror seized Gabriel, as if, at the very hour of his hoped for triumph, some impalpable and vindictive being were gathering forces against him. <break time="0.8s" /> But he shook himself free of it with an effort of reason, and she began to tell him that it had happened one winter, when she was about to leave Galway for a convent in Dublin. <break time="0.8s" /> Michael Furey was ill in his lodgings and was not allowed out, and his people in Oughterard were written to, for it was said that he was in decline, though she never knew for certain. <break time="0.8s" /> Before leaving, she wrote him a letter saying that she was going up to Dublin and would be back in the summer, hoping that he would be better by then.
